claim: The striatum and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) constitute the input stage of the basal ganglia (BG) network.
source: The striatum and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) constitute the input stage of the basal ganglia (BG) network and together innervate BG downstream structures using GABA and glutamate, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is consistent with established neuroanatomical knowledge of the basal ganglia.

claim: The striatum and STN together innervate BG downstream structures using GABA and glutamate, respectively.
source: The striatum and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) constitute the input stage of the basal ganglia (BG) network and together innervate BG downstream structures using GABA and glutamate, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and reflects established knowledge about neurotransmitter systems in the basal ganglia.

claim: Subthalamic activity fluctuations correlate with modulations in the increase/decrease discharge balance of BG downstream neurons during temporal discounting classical condition task.
source: Comparison of the neuronal activity in BG input and downstream structures reveals that subthalamic, not striatal, activity fluctuations correlate with modulations in the increase/decrease discharge balance of BG downstream neurons during temporal discounting classical condition task.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Striatal activity fluctuations do not correlate with modulations in the increase/decrease discharge balance of BG downstream neurons during temporal discounting classical condition task.
source: Comparison of the neuronal activity in BG input and downstream structures reveals that subthalamic, not striatal, activity fluctuations correlate with modulations in the increase/decrease discharge balance of BG downstream neurons during temporal discounting classical condition task.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: After induction of parkinsonism with MPTP, abnormal low beta (8-15 Hz) spiking and local field potential (LFP) oscillations resonate across the BG network.
source: After induction of parkinsonism with 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), abnormal low beta (8-15 Hz) spiking and local field potential (LFP) oscillations resonate across the BG network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 10, 11, and 12.

claim: LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of STN neurons after MPTP treatment.
source: Nevertheless, LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of STN, striatal cholinergic interneurons and BG downstream structures, but do not entrain spiking activity of striatal projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figures 14 and 16.

claim: LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of striatal cholinergic interneurons after MPTP treatment.
source: Nevertheless, LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of STN, striatal cholinergic interneurons and BG downstream structures, but do not entrain spiking activity of striatal projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figures 14 and 16.

claim: LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of BG downstream structures after MPTP treatment.
source: Nevertheless, LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of STN, striatal cholinergic interneurons and BG downstream structures, but do not entrain spiking activity of striatal projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figures 14 and 16.

claim: LFP beta oscillations do not entrain spiking activity of striatal projection neurons after MPTP treatment.
source: Nevertheless, LFP beta oscillations entrain spiking activity of STN, striatal cholinergic interneurons and BG downstream structures, but do not entrain spiking activity of striatal projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figures 14 and 16.

claim: The STN plays a pivotal role in BG physiology and pathophysiology.
source: Our results highlight the pivotal role of STN divergent projections in BG physiology and pathophysiology and may explain why STN is such an effective site for invasive treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease and other BG-related disorders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: STN is an effective site for invasive treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease.
source: Our results highlight the pivotal role of STN divergent projections in BG physiology and pathophysiology and may explain why STN is such an effective site for invasive treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease and other BG-related disorders.
evidence: This is supported by clinical knowledge and cited literature about deep brain stimulation.

claim: State-of-the-art basal ganglia computational models divide the BG network into two functionally related subsystems: the main axis (actor) and the neuromodulators (critics).
source: State-of-the-art basal ganglia (BG) computational models (Gurney et al., 2015; Schultz et al., 1997) divide the BG network into two functionally related subsystems. First, the main axis (or 'actor' in machine learning terminology) which corresponds to the BG structures that connect state-encoding thalamo-cortical areas to cortical and brainstem motor centers. Second, the neuromodulators (machine learning's 'critics', e.g., the midbrain dopaminergic neurons and striatal cholinergic interneurons) that adjust activity along the BG main axis by encoding a prediction error signal capable of modulating the efficacy of cortico-striatal transmission (Deffains and Bergman, 2015; Reynolds et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to computational models.

claim: The BG main axis connects state-encoding thalamo-cortical areas to cortical and brainstem motor centers.
source: First, the main axis (or 'actor' in machine learning terminology) which corresponds to the BG structures that connect state-encoding thalamo-cortical areas to cortical and brainstem motor centers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and reflects established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons and striatal cholinergic interneurons are neuromodulators that adjust activity along the BG main axis.
source: Second, the neuromodulators (machine learning's 'critics', e.g., the midbrain dopaminergic neurons and striatal cholinergic interneurons) that adjust activity along the BG main axis by encoding a prediction error signal capable of modulating the efficacy of cortico-striatal transmission (Deffains and Bergman, 2015; Reynolds et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The striatum and STN receive considerable glutamatergic inputs from the cortex and the thalamus.
source: The input structures of the BG main axis (the striatum and subthalamic nucleus, STN) receive considerable glutamatergic inputs from the cortex and the thalamus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and reflects established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The striatum provides major inhibitory GABAergic drive to the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) and the BG output structures (GPi/SNr).
source: The striatum and STN provide major inhibitory GABAergic and excitatory glutamatergic drive respectively to the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) and the BG output structures (internal segment of the globus pallidus and substantia nigra reticulata, GPi/SNr) (Parent and Hazrati, 1995a, 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to anatomical literature.

claim: The STN provides major excitatory glutamatergic drive to the GPe and the BG output structures (GPi/SNr).
source: The striatum and STN provide major inhibitory GABAergic and excitatory glutamatergic drive respectively to the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) and the BG output structures (internal segment of the globus pallidus and substantia nigra reticulata, GPi/SNr) (Parent and Hazrati, 1995a, 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to anatomical literature.

claim: The GPe emits feedback GABAergic projections to the STN.
source: In return, the GPe emits feedback GABAergic projections to the STN (Carpenter et al., 1981) and the striatum (Hegeman et al., 2016; Mallet et al., 2012) as well as massive feedforward GABAergic projections to the GPi/SNr (Parent and Hazrati, 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to anatomical literature.

claim: The GPe emits feedback GABAergic projections to the striatum.
source: In return, the GPe emits feedback GABAergic projections to the STN (Carpenter et al., 1981) and the striatum (Hegeman et al., 2016; Mallet et al., 2012) as well as massive feedforward GABAergic projections to the GPi/SNr (Parent and Hazrati, 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to anatomical literature.

claim: The GPe emits massive feedforward GABAergic projections to the GPi/SNr.
source: In return, the GPe emits feedback GABAergic projections to the STN (Carpenter et al., 1981) and the striatum (Hegeman et al., 2016; Mallet et al., 2012) as well as massive feedforward GABAergic projections to the GPi/SNr (Parent and Hazrati, 1995b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to anatomical literature.

claim: Degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease leads to striatal dopamine depletion.
source: Traditionally, in Parkinson's disease (PD), it is assumed that degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons leads to striatal dopamine depletion which provokes a cascade of physiological disturbances in the BG main axis, notably the emergence of synchronized oscillatory activity in the BG and cortical networks (Levy et al., 2002; Nini et al., 1995; Oswal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to literature on Parkinson's disease pathophysiology.

claim: Striatal dopamine depletion provokes the emergence of synchronized oscillatory activity in the BG and cortical networks in Parkinson's disease.
source: Traditionally, in Parkinson's disease (PD), it is assumed that degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons leads to striatal dopamine depletion which provokes a cascade of physiological disturbances in the BG main axis, notably the emergence of synchronized oscillatory activity in the BG and cortical networks (Levy et al., 2002; Nini et al., 1995; Oswal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to literature on Parkinson's disease pathophysiology.

claim: Abnormal oscillations in Parkinson's disease likely compromise information flow through the BG main axis.
source: These abnormal oscillations likely compromise information flow through the BG main axis and result in the release of abnormal commands by BG output structures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction based on the literature.

claim: The striatum is the main site of dopamine depletion in human patients and animal models of PD.
source: Despite evidence of subthalamic dopamine depletion in PD and its role in the pathophysiology of the disease (Francois et al., 2000; Galvan et al., 2014; Rommelfanger and Wichmann, 2010), the striatum remains the main site of dopamine depletion in human patients and animal models of PD.
evidence: This is stated with citations to literature on Parkinson's disease.

claim: The striatum is much larger than the STN (107 vs. 105 neurons in non-human primates).
source: In addition, the striatum is much larger than the STN (107 vs. 105 neurons in non-human primates, respectively, Hardman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to anatomical literature.

claim: The STN is the prime target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) of human patients with advanced PD.
source: Nevertheless, the STN, not the striatum, is the prime target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) of human patients with advanced PD (Limousin et al., 1998; Odekerken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to clinical literature on DBS.

claim: STN-DBS abolishes abnormal synchronized oscillations in the BG network of animal models of PD.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that STN-DBS abolishes abnormal synchronized oscillations in the BG network of animal models of PD (Meissner et al., 2005) and human PD patients (Kühn et al., 2008; Wingeier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to experimental literature.

claim: STN-DBS abolishes abnormal synchronized oscillations in the BG network of human PD patients.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that STN-DBS abolishes abnormal synchronized oscillations in the BG network of animal models of PD (Meissner et al., 2005) and human PD patients (Kühn et al., 2008; Wingeier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to clinical literature.

claim: Two monkeys were used in the study.
source: To tackle these issues, we recorded the neuronal activity of the BG input and downstream (central and output) structures of two monkeys engaged in a classical temporal discounting conditioning task (i.e., normal/healthy state, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in the methods.

claim: Neuronal activity was recorded in the normal/healthy state while monkeys were engaged in a temporal discounting classical conditioning task.
source: To tackle these issues, we recorded the neuronal activity of the BG input and downstream (central and output) structures of two monkeys engaged in a classical temporal discounting conditioning task (i.e., normal/healthy state, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neuronal activity was recorded after systemic induction of PD symptoms with MPTP.
source: Then, once we completed the recordings in the normal state, we proceeded to record neuronal activity in the BG network of the same two monkeys after systemic induction of PD symptoms (i.e., parkinsonian state) with 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The animals learned the cue values (appetitive, aversive or neutral).
source: Remarkably, the animals responded with appropriate anticipatory licking and blinking behavior to the outcome delivery in the immediate condition. In contrast, in the delayed condition, the animals did not display any robust anticipatory licking and blinking movements during the cue and delay periods. Together, these behavioral results indicate that the animals learned the cue values (appetitive, aversive or neutral) and differentiated between cues predicting an immediate or a delayed outcome.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B.

claim: The animals differentiated between cues predicting an immediate or a delayed outcome.
source: Together, these behavioral results indicate that the animals learned the cue values (appetitive, aversive or neutral) and differentiated between cues predicting an immediate or a delayed outcome.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B.

claim: The introduction of a 6-s delay period after cue offset probably compromised the temporal predictability of the outcome delivery in the delayed condition.
source: However, the introduction of a 6-s delay period after cue offset probably compromised the temporal predictability of the outcome delivery in the delayed condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The average population response to the cue of each neuronal assembly of the BG main axis persisted until the outcome delivery in both conditions (immediate and delayed).
source: These absolute PSTHs revealed that the average population response to the cue of each neuronal assembly of the BG main axis persisted until the outcome delivery in both conditions (immediate and delayed) (Figure 3, green lines).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Persistent modulations of activity along the BG main axis temporally bridged sensory visual information and the actions wired to outcome delivery.
source: Therefore, these persistent modulations of activity along the BG main axis temporally bridged sensory visual information (provided by cue presentation) and the actions (licking and blinking movements) wired to outcome delivery and continued even when the visual information was no longer available during the 6-s delay period in the delayed condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The persistent responses in the BG main axis contrast with the transient response of the TANs to the cue onset.
source: The persistent responses in the BG main axis contrast with the transient response of the TANs (i.e., one of the BG neuromodulators) to the cue onset (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: For each neuronal assembly of the BG main axis, the absolute response of the population was systematically larger than the relative response.
source: For each neuronal assembly of the BG main axis, the absolute response of the population was systematically larger than the relative response (Figure 3), thus suggesting in line with previous studies (Adler et al., 2012; Espinosa-Parrilla et al., 2013; Joshua et al., 2009b; Turner and Anderson, 2005) that single neuronal responses in the BG main axis consist of either increases or decreases in the firing rate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Single neuronal responses in the BG main axis consist of either increases or decreases in the firing rate.
source: For each neuronal assembly of the BG main axis, the absolute response of the population was systematically larger than the relative response (Figure 3), thus suggesting in line with previous studies (Adler et al., 2012; Espinosa-Parrilla et al., 2013; Joshua et al., 2009b; Turner and Anderson, 2005) that single neuronal responses in the BG main axis consist of either increases or decreases in the firing rate.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Neurons of the BG main axis exhibited diverse patterns in timing and polarity (increase/decrease) of discharge modulations.
source: We found that neurons of the BG main axis exhibited diverse patterns in timing and polarity (increase/decrease) of discharge modulations rather than coordinated sustained modulations of the discharge rate (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The fraction of neurons that modulated their activity at each time bin systematically exceeded chance level for all neuronal assemblies of the BG main axis in both conditions.
source: In both conditions, we also found that the fraction of neurons that modulated their activity (regardless of the polarity of the modulation) at each time bin (20 ms), from cue onset to outcome delivery, systematically exceeded chance level (i.e., p<0.05, the values lay beyond two standard deviations of the mean, empirical 68-95-99.7 rule) for all neuronal assemblies of the BG main axis (Figure 5, left and center histograms).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: ANOVA revealed a significant effect of task period on the fraction of responsive bins for all neuronal assemblies of the BG main axis except for striatal MSNs.
source: Except for striatal MSNs, analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed a significant effect of task period (cue in the immediate condition and cue and delay in the delayed condition) on the fraction of responsive bins (one-way ANOVA, p<0.001) for all other neuronal assemblies of the BG main axis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The fractions of responsive bins in the STN and downstream structures decreased during the delay period.
source: The fractions of responsive bins in the STN and downstream structures decreased during the delay period (p<0.001, post hoc comparisons, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 5, right bar graphs).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The fraction of modulated MSNs remained unchanged over time.
source: Thus, while the fraction of modulated MSNs remained unchanged over time, STN, GPe, GPi and SNr neurons exhibited comparable changes following cue offset in the delayed condition.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: During the cue periods in both conditions, increases in activity strongly predominated in all BG structures.
source: We found that during the cue periods in both conditions, increases in activity (positive I/D balance) strongly predominated in all BG structures (Figure 6, right bar plots).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: During the delay period, the I/D balance was still strikingly biased towards increases in activity for the MSNs.
source: In contrast, during the delay period, although the I/D balance was still strikingly biased towards increases in activity for the MSNs, this imbalance was significantly reduced in the STN and reversed in the GPe, GPi and SNr (one-way ANOVA, p<0.001, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, Figure 6, right bar plots).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: During the delay period, the I/D balance was significantly reduced in the STN.
source: In contrast, during the delay period, although the I/D balance was still strikingly biased towards increases in activity for the MSNs, this imbalance was significantly reduced in the STN and reversed in the GPe, GPi and SNr (one-way ANOVA, p<0.001, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, Figure 6, right bar plots).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: During the delay period, the I/D balance reversed in the GPe, GPi and SNr.
source: In contrast, during the delay period, although the I/D balance was still strikingly biased towards increases in activity for the MSNs, this imbalance was significantly reduced in the STN and reversed in the GPe, GPi and SNr (one-way ANOVA, p<0.001, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, Figure 6, right bar plots).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The inhibitory GABAergic drive from the striatum was unchanged over the different task periods.
source: Thus, whereas the inhibitory GABAergic drive from the striatum was unchanged over the different task periods, the STN excitatory glutamatergic drive was reduced when moving from the cue to the delay periods.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The STN excitatory glutamatergic drive was reduced when moving from the cue to the delay periods.
source: Thus, whereas the inhibitory GABAergic drive from the striatum was unchanged over the different task periods, the STN excitatory glutamatergic drive was reduced when moving from the cue to the delay periods.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The reduced STN excitatory drive was concurrent with a reduction in the activity in the BG downstream structures.
source: This reduced STN excitatory drive was concurrent with a reduction in the activity in the BG downstream structures (Figures 3, 5 and 6) and with the animals' modified behavioral policy (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: Increases dominated during the cue periods in both conditions for all BG neuronal populations.
source: We found that increases dominated during the cue periods in both conditions (χ2 test, p<0.05, for each BG neuronal population, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: During the delay period, increases remained preponderant for striatal MSNs.
source: During the delay period, except for striatal MSNs where increases remained preponderant (χ2 test, p<0.001, Figure 7A), this dominance of the increases disappeared for STN, GPe and GPi neurons and decreases even became dominant for SNr neurons (χ2 test, p<0.001, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: During the delay period, the dominance of increases disappeared for STN, GPe and GPi neurons.
source: During the delay period, except for striatal MSNs where increases remained preponderant (χ2 test, p<0.001, Figure 7A), this dominance of the increases disappeared for STN, GPe and GPi neurons and decreases even became dominant for SNr neurons (χ2 test, p<0.001, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: During the delay period, decreases became dominant for SNr neurons.
source: During the delay period, except for striatal MSNs where increases remained preponderant (χ2 test, p<0.001, Figure 7A), this dominance of the increases disappeared for STN, GPe and GPi neurons and decreases even became dominant for SNr neurons (χ2 test, p<0.001, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For each task period, two-way ANOVA revealed a significant and systematic effect of the BG input (striatum vs. STN) on the similarity coefficient of the neuronal responses of the BG input-downstream neuron pairs.
source: Remarkably, for each task period, two-way ANOVA revealed a significant and systematic effect of the BG input (striatum vs. STN) on the similarity coefficient of the neuronal responses of the BG input-downstream neuron pairs (two-way ANOVA, p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Subthalamic increases correlated with BG downstream increases and decreases.
source: For each task period, we found that subthalamic, rather than striatal (MSN), increases correlated with BG downstream increases (Inc-Inc pairs) and decreases (Inc-Dec pairs), while striatal and subthalamic decreases (although there was a significant BG input effect) correlated almost to an equal extent with BG downstream neuronal responses, regardless of their principal polarity (both Dec-Dec and Dec-Inc pairs).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Subthalamic neuronal responses (increases or decreases) were more strongly correlated to the BG downstream neuronal responses than striatal MSN neuronal responses.
source: However, given the relatively low fraction of striatal decreases (Figure 7A), we concluded that subthalamic, but not striatal MSN, neuronal responses (increases or decreases) were more strongly correlated to the BG downstream neuronal responses, regardless of their polarity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Systemic MPTP injections were used to induce a severe parkinsonian state.
source: We used systemic MPTP injections (see Materials and methods) to induce a severe parkinsonian state.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: F-18 FDOPA positron emission tomography revealed large dopamine depletion in the dorsal striatum following the MPTP treatment.
source: F-18 FDOPA positron emission tomography (Monkey K, Figure 8A, right) and post-mortem tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry (Monkey S, Figure 8B, right) revealed large dopamine depletion in the dorsal striatum (i.e., caudate nucleus and putamen) following the MPTP treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Post-mortem tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry revealed large dopamine depletion in the dorsal striatum following the MPTP treatment.
source: F-18 FDOPA positron emission tomography (Monkey K, Figure 8A, right) and post-mortem tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry (Monkey S, Figure 8B, right) revealed large dopamine depletion in the dorsal striatum (i.e., caudate nucleus and putamen) following the MPTP treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The animals developed all major motor signs of PD, including bradykinesia/akinesia, rigidity, abnormal flexed posture and low-frequency tremor.
source: Our animals developed all major motor signs of PD, including bradykinesia/akinesia, rigidity, abnormal flexed posture and low-frequency tremor (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9.

claim: In the parkinsonian state, the animals were unable to execute the behavioral task and all recordings were made in a quiet alert state.
source: In the parkinsonian state, given the severity of the motor symptoms, the animals were unable to execute the behavioral task and all recordings were made in a quiet alert state.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Comparison of the mean PSDs of the MUA at the different stages of the BG main axis before and after MPTP intoxication revealed the emergence of 8–15 Hz oscillations in the STN, GPe and SNr.
source: Comparison of the mean power spectral densities (PSDs) of the MUA at the different stages of the BG main axis before and after MPTP intoxication revealed the emergence of 8–15 Hz oscillations in the STN, GPe and SNr (GPi activity was not recorded in the MPTP-treated monkeys), but not in the recordings from the areas surrounding the striatal MSNs (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: 8–15 Hz oscillations did not emerge in the recordings from the areas surrounding the striatal MSNs after MPTP intoxication.
source: Comparison of the mean power spectral densities (PSDs) of the MUA at the different stages of the BG main axis before and after MPTP intoxication revealed the emergence of 8–15 Hz oscillations in the STN, GPe and SNr (GPi activity was not recorded in the MPTP-treated monkeys), but not in the recordings from the areas surrounding the striatal MSNs (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The distributions of the oscillation frequencies were similar for the STN, GPe and SNr, with peaks at 10 Hz.
source: The distributions of the oscillation frequencies were similar for the STN, GPe and SNr, and peaks of the distribution were found at 10 Hz for the three structures (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: 10 Hz oscillations of striatal TANs were found after MPTP treatment.
source: Despite the absence of significant oscillations in MSN spiking activity (comprising > 95% of the striatal cells) in the dopamine-depleted striatum, we also found 10 Hz oscillations of striatal TANs after MPTP treatment (Figure 10B, insets), indicating that abnormal oscillatory activity did not spare the striatum.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The peak values of the PSD of the spiking activity (in the 8–15 Hz range) were significantly higher in parkinsonism than in healthy state for TANs, STN, GPe and SNr neurons.
source: Accordingly, we found that the peak values of the PSD of the spiking activity (in the 8–15 Hz range, see Materials and methods) were significantly higher in parkinsonism (after MPTP) than in healthy state (before MPTP) for TANs, STN, GPe and SNr neurons (two-sample t-test, p<0.01, Figure 11), but not for MSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11.

claim: The peak values of the PSD of the spiking activity (in the 8–15 Hz range) were not significantly higher in parkinsonism than in healthy state for MSNs.
source: Accordingly, we found that the peak values of the PSD of the spiking activity (in the 8–15 Hz range, see Materials and methods) were significantly higher in parkinsonism (after MPTP) than in healthy state (before MPTP) for TANs, STN, GPe and SNr neurons (two-sample t-test, p<0.01, Figure 11), but not for MSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11.

claim: MSNs did not exhibit abnormal oscillatory spiking activity after MPTP treatment.
source: Thus, although low beta (8–15 Hz) oscillations were found in the spiking activity of the STN, downstream BG structures, and even striatal TANs, MSNs (recorded in striatal areas with TAN oscillations) did not exhibit such abnormal oscillatory spiking activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 10 and 11.

claim: After MPTP intoxication, exaggerated 8–15 Hz oscillations of LFPs were found in all BG structures, including the striatum.
source: After MPTP intoxication, we also found exaggerated 8–15 Hz oscillations of local field potentials (LFPs) recorded in all BG structures, including the striatum in the vicinity of both TANs and MSNs (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 12.

claim: Peak coherence values in the 8–15 Hz range increased significantly after MPTP intoxication for all BG neuronal assemblies except MSNs.
source: Estimates of the coherence between spike trains of the isolated units (single-unit activity) and LFPs revealed that except for MSNs, peak coherence values in the 8–15 Hz range increased significantly after MPTP intoxication (two-sample t-test, p<0.001) for all other BG neuronal assemblies (Figure 14, left plots).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 14.

claim: Using spike train of the isolated units or MUA for the calculation of the spike-filed coherence yielded the same qualitative results.
source: We found that using spike train of the isolated units or MUA for the calculation of the spike-filed coherence yielded the same qualitative results.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 14 and Figure 14—figure supplement 1.

claim: After MPTP intoxication, TAN, STN, GPe and SNr neurons tended to fire around the negative peak of the 8–15 Hz oscillatory LFP.
source: Calculation of the phase of the spiking activity relative to the LFP at the frequency of the coherence peak values in the 8–15 Hz range revealed that LFP relative phase values of the single-unit (Figure 14, right polar histograms) and multi-unit (Figure 14—figure supplement 1, right polar histograms) spiking activity of TAN, STN, GPe and SNr neurons mainly ranged from 180 to 270º. Namely, TAN, STN, GPe and SNr neurons tended to fire around the negative peak of the 8–15 Hz oscillatory LFP - but see Nelson and Pouget (2010) for possible confounding effects of electrode and instrument filter properties on the exact phase relationships between spikes and LFPs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 14.

claim: The STA LFP analysis revealed that except for MSNs, the coincidence between the spikes of the STN, GPe, SNr neurons, as well as those of the TANs, and the negative waves of the LFP oscillations increased after MPTP intoxication.
source: The STA LFP analysis revealed that except for MSNs, the coincidence between the spikes of the STN, GPe, SNr neurons, as well as those of the TANs, and the negative waves of the LFP oscillations increased after MPTP intoxication (Figure 16, left and central columns).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 16.

claim: The random dilution of the spike trains did not affect the STA-LFP results.
source: We found that the random dilution of the spike trains did not affect the STA-LFP results (Figure 16, right column).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 16.

claim: In the parkinsonian state, spike-LFP synchronization was not influenced by the firing rate of BG neuronal components.
source: Therefore, in the parkinsonian state, spike-LFP synchronization was not influenced by the firing rate of BG neuronal components and more importantly, the absence of phase locking between MSN spiking activity and striatal LFPs was probably not due to the confounding effects of the slow discharge rate of the MSNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 16.

claim: The absence of phase locking between MSN spiking activity and striatal LFPs was probably not due to the confounding effects of the slow discharge rate of the MSNs.
source: Therefore, in the parkinsonian state, spike-LFP synchronization was not influenced by the firing rate of BG neuronal components and more importantly, the absence of phase locking between MSN spiking activity and striatal LFPs was probably not due to the confounding effects of the slow discharge rate of the MSNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 16.

claim: Persistent population activity in the BG main axis may form a persistent internal representation.
source: Hence, in each neuronal assembly of the BG main axis, a modulation of the population activity may form a persistent internal representation (Curtis and Lee, 2010; Durstewitz et al., 2000; Goldman-Rakic, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to literature on working memory.

claim: The BG persistent population activity reflects the neuronal coupling between the current state and the upcoming contingent behavioral response.
source: Our working hypothesis holds that the BG persistent population activity reflects the neuronal coupling between the current state (defined by cue presentation) and the upcoming contingent behavioral response (licking or blinking movement in our task).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: The heterogeneity of the BG main axis responses contrasts with the homogeneity of the transient responses of the BG neuromodulators.
source: The heterogeneity of the BG main axis responses (Adler et al., 2012; Deffains et al., 2010; Joshua et al., 2009a) contrasts with the homogeneity of the transient responses of the BG neuromodulators (Graybiel et al., 1994; Joshua et al., 2009a) and corroborates the view that the BG main axis has a large information capacity that can encode the enormous and diverse possibilities of state-to-action mapping (Bar-Gad et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: The BG main axis has a large information capacity that can encode the enormous and diverse possibilities of state-to-action mapping.
source: The heterogeneity of the BG main axis responses (Adler et al., 2012; Deffains et al., 2010; Joshua et al., 2009a) contrasts with the homogeneity of the transient responses of the BG neuromodulators (Graybiel et al., 1994; Joshua et al., 2009a) and corroborates the view that the BG main axis has a large information capacity that can encode the enormous and diverse possibilities of state-to-action mapping (Bar-Gad et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: The fluctuations in STN activity were concurrent with the modifications of activity in the BG downstream network, without apparent parallel modulations of striatal activity.
source: Here, we found that in the normal awake monkey engaged in a temporal discounting classical conditioning task, the fluctuations in STN activity were concurrent with the modifications of activity in the BG downstream network, without apparent parallel modulations of striatal activity (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Examination of the temporal patterns of changes in activity in the MSN assembly did not indicate the presence of two distinct sub-populations.
source: However, examination of the temporal patterns of changes in activity in the MSN assembly did not indicate the presence of two distinct sub-populations (Figures 3, 4, 5 and 6), which is consistent with recent studies revealing the co-activation of the striatal direct and indirect pathways (Cui et al., 2013; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to recent studies.

claim: Recent studies reveal the co-activation of the striatal direct and indirect pathways.
source: However, examination of the temporal patterns of changes in activity in the MSN assembly did not indicate the presence of two distinct sub-populations (Figures 3, 4, 5 and 6), which is consistent with recent studies revealing the co-activation of the striatal direct and indirect pathways (Cui et al., 2013; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to recent studies.

claim: Information transfer via the hyper-direct pathway is faster and more broadly distributed in the BG output structures than the information flowing along the direct and indirect pathways.
source: Although there is an ongoing debate on the distribution of STN output in the BG downstream network (Mathai and Smith, 2011; Sato et al., 2000), a compelling functional model of action selection process in the BG network claims that information transfer via the hyper-direct (cortex-STN-GPi/SNr) pathway is faster and more broadly distributed in the BG output structures than the information flowing along the direct and indirect (striatum-GPi/SNr) pathways (Mink, 1996; Nambu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to functional models.

claim: The STN might orchestrate the time-varying I/D balance in the BG downstream network.
source: Given that the striatum and the STN are the two input structures of the BG network and that STN neuronal responses were more strongly correlated with BG downstream neuronal responses, compared to striatal MSN responses (Figure 7B), we suggest that the STN might orchestrate the time-varying I/D balance in the BG downstream network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The STN would exert a powerful glutamatergic and apparently GABAergic striatal-free control over the release of BG output commands.
source: Thus, the STN would exert a powerful glutamatergic and apparently GABAergic striatal-free control over the release of BG output commands (Baunez et al., 2001; Frank et al., 2007a; Jahanshahi et al., 2015) prior to their fine modulation by the direct and indirect pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: This specific correlation between the divergent excitatory STN projections and BG downstream neurons was only shown for a classical conditioning task with immediate and delayed outcomes.
source: Nonetheless, this specific correlation between the divergent excitatory STN projections and BG downstream neurons was only shown here for a classical conditioning task with immediate and delayed outcomes and should be tested in the future under a range of behavioral conditions and paradigms.
evidence: This is a limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: A harsh MPTP intoxication procedure was used to induce a large striatal dopamine depletion and guarantee the emergence of the full spectrum of pathological synchronous oscillations in the BG.
source: In this study, we used a harsh MPTP intoxication procedure (see Materials and methods) rather than a slower regimen of MPTP intoxication (i.e., that would have led to a L-DOPA responsive parkinsonian monkey capable of executing behavioral tasks). This decision was made to induce a large striatal dopamine depletion (Figure 8) and guarantee the emergence of the full spectrum of pathological synchronous oscillations in the BG.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Earlier studies have failed to find abnormal BG oscillatory activity at the early stage of chronic MPTP treatment.
source: Indeed, earlier studies have failed to find abnormal BG oscillatory activity at the early stage of chronic MPTP treatment (Leblois et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to previous studies.

claim: Severe MPTP-treated monkeys usually develop stable clinical symptoms.
source: Therefore, we favored severe MPTP-treated monkeys that usually develop stable clinical symptoms (Potts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to previous studies.

claim: Abnormal spiking oscillatory activity after MPTP intoxication of African green monkeys occurred in the low beta (8–15 Hz) range.
source: In line with earlier studies conducted on MPTP-treated monkeys (Bergman et al., 1994; Raz et al., 2001; Soares et al., 2004), we found that abnormal spiking oscillatory activity after MPTP intoxication of African green monkeys (vervets) occurred in the low beta (8–15 Hz) range.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: MSNs apparently failed to express pathological 8–15 Hz neuronal oscillations, as did the STN and BG downstream structures.
source: Even though earlier rodent (Costa et al., 2006) and primate (Singh et al., 2015) studies have shown that MSN activity patterns are altered in parkinsonism, we found that MSNs apparently failed to express pathological 8–15 Hz neuronal oscillations, as did the STN and BG downstream structures (Figures 10 and 11).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 10 and 11.

claim: The lack of oscillatory activity of MSNs in the MPTP-treated monkey is consistent with unpublished observations of no oscillatory spiking activity in the striatum of parkinsonian human patients undergoing DBS procedures.
source: The lack of oscillatory activity of MSNs in the MPTP-treated monkey is consistent with our unpublished observations of no oscillatory spiking activity in the striatum of parkinsonian human patients undergoing DBS procedures.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: TANs exhibited 10 Hz oscillatory activity after MPTP intoxication.
source: However, not all components of striatal activity were deprived of abnormal oscillatory activity after MPTP intoxication. Indeed, as already described in earlier studies of TANs in MPTP-treated monkeys (Raz et al., 1996), we found that TANs also exhibited 10 Hz oscillatory activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to previous studies.

claim: The MSN-TAN incongruity is in line with the view of a weak functional in vivo connectivity between MSNs and TANs.
source: This MSN-TAN incongruity is in line with the view of a weak functional in vivo connectivity between MSNs and TANs (Adler et al., 2013b) and probably reflects their different synaptic drives.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to previous studies.

claim: 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations were also observed in the healthy state (before MPTP).
source: Nevertheless, 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations (although sparser) were also observed in the healthy state (before MPTP).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 12.

claim: In normal behavior control, beta oscillatory activity is known to play a role in the maintenance of the current sensorimotor or cognitive state.
source: In normal behavior control, beta oscillatory activity is known to play a role in the maintenance of the current sensorimotor or cognitive state (the status quo) (Brittain and Brown, 2014; Engel and Fries, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to literature on beta oscillations.

claim: The 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations observed in the healthy state likely correspond to one of the neuronal processes involved in state-to-action mapping.
source: Therefore, the 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations observed in the healthy state likely correspond to one of the neuronal processes involved in state-to-action mapping.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: Exaggeration of 8–15 Hz oscillatory activity after induction of parkinsonism would compromise the ability of human PD patients to adjust their behavior to situational demands.
source: Consequently, exaggeration of 8–15 Hz oscillatory activity after induction of parkinsonism would compromise the ability of human PD patients to adjust their behavior to situational demands (Brown and Marsden, 1988; Cools et al., 1984; Frank et al., 2007b) due to an abnormal persistence of the BG 'status quo' signal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to clinical literature.

claim: The dopamine-depleted striatum was bombarded with pathological oscillations by its major afferent neurons.
source: Thus, as for other structures in the closed loop of the BG network, we found that the dopamine-depleted striatum was also bombarded with pathological oscillations by its major afferent neurons (Figure 12).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 12.

claim: Striatal oscillating synaptic inputs apparently only entrained the spiking activity of the TANs, but not the MSNs.
source: However, these striatal oscillating synaptic inputs apparently only entrained the spiking activity of the TANs, but not the MSNs (Figures 10 and 11).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 10 and 11.

claim: After MPTP intoxication, there was no evidence for a linear relationship between the strength of the 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations and the degree of spike-field coherence in the 8–15 Hz range along the BG network.
source: After MPTP intoxication, we found no evidence for a (linear) relationship between the strength of the 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations and the degree of spike-field coherence in the 8–15 Hz range (Figure 15 and Figure 15—figure supplement 1) along the BG network.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 15.

claim: Whatever the strength of the 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations within the striatum, MSN spiking activity failed to lock with these LFP oscillations.
source: Therefore, whatever the strength of the 8–15 Hz LFP oscillations within the striatum, MSN spiking activity failed to lock with these LFP oscillations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 15.

claim: The abnormal striatal synaptic inputs may not have been strong enough to depolarize the membrane potential of the MSNs above the spike threshold.
source: Rather, the abnormal striatal synaptic inputs may not have been strong enough to depolarize the membrane potential of the MSNs above the spike threshold.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: The classical rate model of the BG network predicts that striatal dopamine depletion leads to a reduction of the D1-MSM discharge and an elevation of the D2-MSN discharge.
source: Based on the classical rate model of the BG network (Albin et al., 1989; Bergman et al., 1990; Gerfen et al., 1990), striatal dopamine depletion leads to a reduction of the D1-MSM discharge and an elevation of the D2-MSN discharge.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to the classical rate model.

claim: No robust increase in the firing rate of the MSNs recorded within the dopamine-depleted striatum was found.
source: In contrast to an earlier study (Liang et al., 2008), we did not find any robust increase in the firing rate of the MSNs recorded within the dopamine-depleted striatum (Figure 17).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 17.

claim: After MPTP intoxication, the firing rate decreased in the GPe and increased in the STN.
source: However, in agreement with earlier studies (Bergman et al., 1994; Filion and Tremblay, 1991; Miller and DeLong, 1987), we also found that after MPTP intoxication, the firing rate decreased in the GPe and increased in the STN (Figure 17).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 17.

claim: The slight elevation of the striatal GABAergic drive to the GPe may have induced oscillatory activity in the BG downstream structures.
source: Therefore, we cannot rule out the possibility that the slight elevation of the striatal GABAergic drive to the GPe (via D2-MSNs, Figure 2A) may have induced oscillatory activity in the BG downstream structures (Terman et al., 2002), probably through changes in the activity pattern of the GPe-STN closed circuit (Bevan et al., 2002; Plenz and Kital, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to computational models.

claim: Despite the abnormal oscillating synaptic inputs in the striatum, striatal projection neurons (MSNs) failed to express spiking (output) activity.
source: Noticeably, despite the abnormal oscillating synaptic inputs in the striatum, striatal projection neurons (MSNs) failed to express spiking (output) activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 10, 11, 14, and 16.

claim: Abnormal oscillatory activity within dopamine-depleted striatum did not propagate to the BG downstream structures.
source: Therefore, abnormal oscillatory activity within dopamine-depleted striatum did not propagate to the BG downstream structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: The abnormal oscillations observed in PD resonate across the closed loop of the cortico-BG network through the STN, not the striatum.
source: Therefore, our results are in line with other studies (Nambu and Tachibana, 2014) and suggest that the abnormal oscillations observed in PD resonate across the closed loop of the cortico-BG network through the STN, not the striatum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data with a citation to previous studies.

claim: The STN may be the driving force behind the physiology as well as the pathophysiology of the BG.
source: Overall, the current study conducted on both normal and parkinsonian animals support the idea that the STN may be the driving force behind the physiology (Kitai and Kita, 1987) as well as the pathophysiology of the BG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data with a citation to previous studies.

claim: The striatum remains a major player in BG functioning in health and disease.
source: Nevertheless, the striatum obviously remains a major player in BG functioning in health and disease.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Striatal dopaminergic input is involved in the modulation of the efficacy of the cortico-striatal synapses.
source: Striatal dopaminergic input is involved not only in the modulation of the efficacy of the cortico-striatal synapses (Reynolds et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2008), but also in the excitability of the striatal projection neuron (Nicola et al., 2000; Onn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: Striatal dopaminergic input is involved in the excitability of the striatal projection neuron.
source: Striatal dopaminergic input is involved not only in the modulation of the efficacy of the cortico-striatal synapses (Reynolds et al., 2001; Shen et al., 2008), but also in the excitability of the striatal projection neuron (Nicola et al., 2000; Onn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: The coincidence of cortical/thalamic and midbrain dopaminergic activity might be a necessary condition for MSN spike generation.
source: Thus, the coincidence of cortical/thalamic and midbrain dopaminergic activity might be a necessary condition for MSN spike generation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: MSN spiking activity would be shaped by striatal inputs only during brief, but functionally important periods.
source: Consequently, MSN spiking activity would be shaped by striatal inputs only during brief, but functionally important periods (probably marked by transient dopaminergic activity).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: This refined control of striatal output patterns was probably undetected in the current population analysis.
source: This refined control of striatal output patterns was probably undetected in the current population analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a limitation.

claim: The study of the neuronal activity along the BG network in similar classical (but also operant) conditioning tasks using MPTP-treated monkeys that exhibit moderate parkinsonian symptoms is a necessary step.
source: Therefore, the study of the neuronal activity along the BG network in similar classical (but also operant) conditioning tasks using MPTP-treated monkeys that exhibit moderate parkinsonian symptoms is undoubtedly a necessary step that should enhance our understanding of the physiology and pathophysiology of the BG.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a future direction.

claim: The unique anatomical and physiological features of the STN provide a concrete explanation for the efficacy of the inactivation of the STN in MPTP-treated monkeys.
source: However, the unique anatomical and physiological features of the STN highlighted in the current study provide a concrete explanation for the efficacy of the inactivation of the STN in MPTP-treated monkeys (Bergman et al., 1990), human patients (Alvarez et al., 2005) and STN-DBS in MPTP-treated monkeys (Benazzouz et al., 1993) and parkinsonian patients to alleviate BG-related motor (Odekerken et al., 2016) and non-motor (Lhommée et al., 2012) clinical symptoms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data with citations to previous studies.

claim: Two female African vervet green monkeys weighing ~4 kg were used in the study.
source: Two female African vervet green monkeys (K and S, Cercopithecus aethiops aethiops), weighing ~4 kg, were trained in a temporal discounting classical conditioning task (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.

claim: Six different fractal visual cues were presented for 2 s in the task.
source: Six different fractal visual cues were presented for 2 s.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.

claim: Cues predicted either a food outcome, an airpuff outcome, or neither of them.
source: Cues predicted either a food outcome, an airpuff outcome (directed at both eyes) or neither of them, thus grouping them into three categories: appetitive/rewarding, aversive and neutral cues.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.

claim: The outcome period lasted 0.15 s.
source: The outcome period (0.15 s) was signaled by one of three sounds that differentiated the three possible outcomes (food, airpuff or no outcome) and was followed by a variable inter-trial interval (ITI) of 6–10 s.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.

claim: The inter-trial interval was 6–10 s.
source: The outcome period (0.15 s) was signaled by one of three sounds that differentiated the three possible outcomes (food, airpuff or no outcome) and was followed by a variable inter-trial interval (ITI) of 6–10 s.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.

claim: Five IM injections of 0.35 mg/kg/injection MPTP were made over the course of four days.
source: Five IM injections of 0.35 mg/kg/injection were made over the course of four days (two injections in the first day) under Ketamine (10 mg/kg IM) sedation.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.

claim: Neuronal recordings during the parkinsonian state began when the animal exhibited severe parkinsonian symptoms, 7 days after the first injection.
source: Neuronal recordings during the parkinsonian state began when the animal exhibited severe parkinsonian symptoms, 7 days after the first injection (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods.
